title: Global Optimization of Large-Scale Extended and Generalized Pooling Problems: Mixed-Integer Nonlinearly Constrained Models
contribution: Four-page TOGO 2010 extended abstract (with Floudas) summarising two pooling lines: the EPA Complex Emissions-extended pooling MINLP solved to global optimality with piecewise-linear and edge-concave relaxations in branch and bound, and generalized pooling (topology as decision) solved up to 15 plants to 0.1% gap, about forty times faster than the prior best.
problem_entry: Standard pooling made harder along two real-world axes: appending the EPA Title 40 CFR 80.45 Complex Emissions Model as constraints, and making network topology a decision variable (pp. 97-98).
key_idea: Assemble known relaxations (piecewise-linear for bilinear terms, edge-concave, McCormick, RLT) plus branching and bounds tightening into one branch and bound and push it to large instances; partitioning level chosen from experience with the topology (pp. 98-99).
assumptions: Linear blending gives bilinear terms; standard pooling is a non-convexifiable QCQP; EPA model adds multilinear, exponential and power-law terms; binary pipe/node activation gives a nonconvex MINLP with quadratic equalities (pp. 97-98).
experiments: Extended pooling: 3 cases up to 1104 continuous/150 binary variables and 640 nonlinear terms solved to global optimality (Table 1, p. 98); generalized pooling ladder 4/10/15/20 plants: 0.1% gap in 38.25 s, 680.66 s, 2489.76 s (784.81 s on 8 threads), 20-plant at 0.9% and 2.3% gaps; prior best re-run on modern hardware reaches 1.2% in 1561.6 s (pp. 98-99).
positioning: Extends Meyer-Floudas 2006 generalized pooling and Meyer-Floudas 2005 edge-concave envelopes and her own 2009 piecewise-linear comparison; credits Audet et al. 2004 for the problem; cites many contemporary piecewise-linear works; does not cite the two other pooling papers in the same volume (pp. 98, 100; contents pp. 5-6).
writing: Compact, number-driven: the two-item (i)/(ii) list repeated in abstract, introduction and summary; hardness given by size tables with term counts by type; one hedge on transfer from small to large instances; profit/cost inconsistency between abstract and introduction (pp. 97-99).
limits_future: 20-plant instances left at 0.9% and 2.3% gaps; 15-plant solve needed topology-specific choice of partitioning level; suggests small instantiations of a topology for insight into industrial sizes (p. 99).

method_links.note: Weak: the goal is a good global algorithm for the class, built by exploring McCormick, RLT, piecewise-linear, branching and bounds tightening inside B&B; results are whole-algorithm times and gaps; no ablation shown.

Piecewise partitioning level set per topology from experience ('predicting a good partitioning level'), unlike the later one-setting-across-a-class stance; consistent with the stated limitation that choosing N has no theory.
Weak: prior best re-run on modern hardware and software before comparison; unsolved 20-plant instances reported with remaining gaps; no competitor solvers or feasibility re-checks in this text.
Weak: the named pooling structure (bilinear terms from linear blending) is exploited by class-specific relaxations; no detection step.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: 4/10/15/20-plant generalized pooling cases from one wastewater superstructure with eqs/continuous/binary/bilinear counts per rung (Table 2, Figure 1).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: learn settings on small instantiations, transfer to industrial size
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: 15-plant case solved after predicting a good partitioning level from experience with the topology; suggests small instantiations for insight on industrially-sized cases.
EPA Title 40 CFR 80.45 Complex Emissions Model (eleven fuel qualities) appended to the standard pooling problem.

transferable: Build an instance ladder from one superstructure and tabulate equations, continuous, binary and bilinear counts per rung (Table 2, p. 99).
Before claiming a speed-up, re-run the best previous method on current hardware and software and compare time and final gap together (p. 98).
Report the largest instances that do not close with their remaining gap instead of dropping them (p. 99).
Tune a partitioning parameter on small instantiations of the same topology before attacking the industrial size, and say so (p. 99).
Characterise hardness by counting nonlinear terms by type (bilinear only vs all), not only variables (Table 1, p. 98).

quotes.text: The industrially-sized 15-Plant test case was solved to a 0.1% optimality gap after some experience with the particular topology by predicting a good partitioning level for the problem.
We integrated these relaxations into a branch-and-bound algorithm and solved the three test cases summarized in Table 1 to global optimality.
